scenario.figure_or_table: Figure 10 (with Table 3 on PDF page 8 and Figure 8 on PDF page 7)
scenario.description: Steady-state HotSpot 6.0 temperature per layer of the TSV-based 3x3x3 3D-NoC, using the Figure 2(c) layout (TSVs surrounding the router logic), under synthetic benchmarks (Matrix, HotSpot 5%/10%, Uniform, Transpose), compared with the Monolithic 3D-NoC. The text reports a highest Monolithic temperature of 351.64 K (78.49 C). Table 3 gives a 290 um x 290 um router floorplan, 220 um x 220 um router logic and 4.06 um x 4.06 um TSVs. Per-router powers appear only as bar charts (Figure 8) and no block-level x/y coordinates are published, so no complete floorplan/power experiment can be extracted. Decisive mismatches for steady 2D use: the scenario is a 3D stack with bonding/TIM layers, TSV thermal modelling, and a monolithic comparison.
scenario.architecture: 3x3x3 3D Network-on-Chip, TSV-based (compared with Monolithic), 3D mesh routers with 7 ports, 45 nm NanGate library, 1.1 V
scenario.workload: Synthetic NoC traffic benchmarks (Matrix, HotSpot 5% and 10%, Uniform, Transpose) at maximum injection rate; router power from PrimeTime energy per bit combined with flit counts (Equation 3)
scenario.operating_point: 500 MHz, 1.1 V, maximum injection rate; steady-state temperature from HotSpot 6.0; router static power about 7.6e-4 W, energy per bit about 9.25e-13 J/bit

original_setup.solver: HotSpot 6.0 steady-state grid thermal model of the 3x3x3 TSV-based 3D-NoC (Figure 2(c) layout) with a Monolithic comparison. A Black's-model reliability post-process is applied (PDF pages 2, 5, 8, 9).
original_setup.optimizer: None. Layouts (Figure 2(b), Figure 2(c), added thermal TSVs) were compared by hand, with no automated optimizer (PDF pages 4, 9).
original_setup.controller: None. No thermal-management controller is used. Voltage/frequency scaling is only an analytic power-scaling equation (Equations 4 and 5), and transient temperature is mentioned as supported but not evaluated (PDF pages 5, 7).
original_setup.benchmark: Synthetic NoC traffic (Matrix, HotSpot 5%, HotSpot 10%, Uniform, Transpose) at 500 MHz, 1.1 V and maximum injection rate, with gem5 garnet 2.0 PARSEC traffic as the second workload. Router power comes from PrimeTime energy per bit (9.2546e-13 J/bit) combined with flit counts (PDF pages 7, 9).

thermal_observable.location: Hottest point of the Monolithic 3D-NoC under the synthetic benchmarks (Figure 10). The text does not name the layer or router.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Maximum steady-state HotSpot 6.0 temperature reported in the text for the Monolithic system. The aggregation over routers, layers and benchmarks is not fully specified. The text gives 351.64 K = 78.49 C.

physical_mismatches.reason: The scenario is a 3D stack with 3 layers, bonding/TIM layers, and TSV-based inter-layer heat paths. A steady 2D single-die thermal model cannot represent it.
The Monolithic versus TSV-based comparison depends on removing the bonding layers and on the TSV effective thermal resistivity (0.0226 mK/W from Table 3). A standard 2D package does not have these.
The heatsink sits on top of the stack. Lower layers are cooled only through upper layers and TSVs, so the temperature differences between layers are 3D effects.
The reported observable is a per-layer temperature of a 3D stack. Reliability results use Black's model with a Copper TSV activation energy, which is not a thermal solver output.
Per-router powers are published only as bar charts (Figure 8). Power comes from the router energy-per-bit model scaled by flit counts, not from a published per-block power table.
The original paper has no optimizer or controller (no DTM, no placement optimization), so there is nothing to map onto an optimizer or controller in the Studio.

parameters.note: Router static power is 7.66e-4 W in the p7 text but 7.64e-4 W in Table 2 (p7). Energy per bit is 9.246e-13 in the text but 9.2546e-13 in Table 2. Table 2 energy 2.9022496e-8 J / 31360 bits = 9.2547e-13, so the extraction's normalized 9.246e-13 follows the text typo rather than the arithmetically consistent value. Table 3 TSV area '35,700 um2 / 10.16%' is inconsistent with a 290x290 um tile (10.16% is about 8,545 um2) and is unexplained. Table 3 resistivities are plausible as m·K/W: Cu 0.0025 corresponds to 400 W/mK. The extraction still labels them unverified. Table 1 vs text: 1/0.011537 is about 87x, not the stated 220x at 30 C.

assessment.summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable. Studio did not run: the simulation status is skipped, the gate has simulation_allowed false, and comparison_valid is false. The reason given is that a custom experiment needs 1–128 blocks and a power_w object, and the extraction supplied an empty floorplan and empty power map. The paper scenario is the steady-state HotSpot 6.0 per-layer temperature of a TSV-based 3x3x3 3D-NoC (Figure 10), compared with a Monolithic 3D-NoC. The only numeric observable is the text-quoted maximum Monolithic temperature of 351.64 K (78.49 C). Its layer, router and benchmark are not named, and the aggregation is not fully specified. The intended experiment kind was custom_2d_steady, so even if it had run it would have produced a steady result with no transient trace and no bundled EV6/GCC adaptation. There is therefore no Studio temperature to compare with 351.64 K, and no numerical agreement or disagreement can be claimed. The 3D stack physics (three layers, bonding/TIM layers, TSV heat paths, a top-mounted heatsink, a monolithic comparison) cannot be represented by a single-die 2D steady model. The paper's reliability results use Black's model and are not thermal solver outputs. Only qualitative remarks are defensible: in the paper, layer position and TSV or bonding-layer treatment drive temperature differences, which a 2D model would not capture. This assessment does not replicate or validate the paper, and it makes no claim of exact replication.
limitations: Studio was not executed, so no simulated temperature, map or trace exists for this scenario.
